A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UTRL research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite rewriting, relocation, and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original TACO evaluations, comparisons against SFT and CURE, code-generator training results, and validity-reward ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds evaluations of Qwen3-14B trained with UTRL and additional unit-test generation baselines.

M1.justification: The alternating GRPO training, discrimination and validity rewards, ground-truth-code filtering, and code-generator reward remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 and Section 3 reformulate the existing procedure using Pass notation and integrated filtering; they do not introduce a new method component.

E1.justification: Both versions use TACO instruction–Python-code pairs, the CodeContests subset for the matched CURE comparison, and the same TACO competitive-programming evaluation coverage. The additional models do not introduce new datasets, domains, or task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 adds Qwen3-14B and DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite as unit-test generation comparators in Tables 1 and 3 and Figure 4. Qwen3-14B previously participated as a code generator, a different role. CURE and both SFT variants remain; identifying the reasoning-SFT scheme with CodeRM does not add another evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: v2 adds a Qwen3-14B UTRL configuration trained for 100 steps in one iteration. It also changes CURE's stated KL coefficient from 1e-3 in v1 Table 3 to 1e-2 in v2 Table 4, without establishing that CURE was rerun. Existing datasets, splits, and evaluation metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The validity-reward and clipping ablations retain the same curves and findings, moving from v1 Section 4.6/Figure 9 to v2 Appendix A.2/Figure 10. The two-iteration analysis also remains, with its plots split and relocated. No new ablation, robustness test, or substantive diagnostic study is introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The additional result rows retain the existing reporting practice; GRPO's reward normalization is not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds Qwen3-14B UTRL results, including 15.7%/17.1% best-of-32 accuracy with Qwen3-8B/14B code generators and 0.764 fidelity, plus scores for the added baselines. Existing Table 1 results remain. UTRL fidelity changes from 0.746 in v1 Figure 6 to 0.741 in v2 Figure 5; iterative-reward caption gains change from 0.2/0.7 to 0.02/0.07. Code-generator accuracy in the prose changes from 14.1% to 15.3% despite retaining the training curve, so this does not establish a rerun improvement.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 Equation 5 removes the 1/|o| normalization from the background PPO objective, changing its weighting of variable-length completions. The GRPO objective remains unchanged. The main reward equations largely restate existing filtering and weighting, and no theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The central claims remain: UTRL trains unit-test generators without ground-truth test annotations, outperforms SFT and frontier-model baselines, and trains code generators comparably to ground-truth-test rewards. Explicitly naming GPT-4o and adding larger-model evidence do not materially redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 replaces the detailed explanation of reasoning-SFT's fidelity/discrimination tradeoff with an interpretation emphasizing SFT memorization versus RL generalization. A new footnote explains hallucinations when attaching reasoning to existing tests. Appendix A.6 retains the original limitations but adds better exploration through alternative RL algorithms as a proposed remedy for the ground-truth-test performance gap.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix A.3 newly specifies lambda=0.85, the 4B training schedule, validation-based checkpoint selection, and Pass execution checks including a 10-second limit. Appendix A.4 clarifies the 32-code-samples-per-model fidelity evaluation. These are principally additional disclosures. Conversely, v1's available-code URL is removed and replaced by a future commitment to release data, checkpoints, and code; actual external availability cannot be determined from the PDFs.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Chu et al. on SFT/RL generalization, AlphaCode/CodeContests, the Qwen2.5 report, and DeepSeek-Coder-V2. It also explicitly positions the existing reasoning-SFT baseline as a CodeRM replication. The central distinction from CURE remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Sections 3 and 4 undergo extensive explanatory rewriting. v2 reorganizes experimental settings, swaps the code-generator and iterative-training subsections, moves the ablation discussion into the appendix, and restructures implementation and limitations material. Ethics and reproducibility statements are added. This substantially revises the narrative despite a stable method.

P2.justification: v2 expands and regroups comparison tables and the fidelity chart while retaining their basic designs. v1 Figure 7 becomes v2 Figures 8 and 9, with the iteration-comparison bar chart's lower axis limit changing from 10 to 13. The ablation figure moves to the appendix, Algorithm 1 is reformatted, and several displays are relocated or recaptioned.

improvement.justification: The larger-model evaluation, additional baselines, and clearer reward, training, and execution details modestly strengthen the evidence and reproducibility. Correcting the conflicting fidelity value also improves consistency. These benefits are tempered by replacing the code-access URL with a future-release statement and introducing an SFT-memorization interpretation without a direct supporting experiment. The gains remain limited within the unchanged method and task coverage.
